concept.name: Settlement cycle
concept.definition: The standard interval between the trade date and the settlement date for a class of transactions, conventionally written T+n (trade date plus n business days). The SEC shortened the standard settlement cycle for most U.S. broker-dealer securities transactions from T+2 to T+1, effective May 28, 2024.
concept.intuition: The plumbing delay between agreeing a trade and actually exchanging cash for securities — the shorter it is, the less can go wrong in between.
concept.mechanics: During the cycle, trades are matched, confirmed, affirmed, and cleared; obligations are netted and margined; on settlement day, securities and funds move, typically delivery-versus-payment. Shortening the cycle compresses the window in which counterparty, market, and liquidity risks can accumulate.
concept.formula: Settlement date = trade date T + n business days (n = 1 for most U.S. securities since May 28, 2024; n = 2 previously and still in some markets and instruments).
concept.failure_modes: Shorter cycles squeeze operational timelines: affirmation, securities lending recalls, and cross-timezone FX funding (for foreign investors buying U.S. assets) must complete faster, raising fail risk for unprepared participants.
concept.misconceptions: T+1 does not mean you wait a day to use your shares or proceeds in all cases — brokers may credit accounts at execution — and the cycle is a market-standard maximum convention, with same-day and negotiated settlements also existing.
concept.example: A U.S. stock trade executed on Monday, June 3, 2024 settles on Tuesday, June 4 (T+1); the same trade in 2023 would have settled on Wednesday (T+2).

citations.source: SEC Press Release 2023-29, SEC Finalizes Rules to Reduce Risks in Clearance and Settlement
citations.section: Press release (T+2 to T+1; compliance date May 28, 2024)
